ety.text: Clipping of pianoforte, from Italian pianoforte, from piano (“soft”) + forte (“strong”). So named because it could produce a wide range of varied volumes note-by-note, in contrast to older keyboard instruments, notably the harpsichord. Doublet of llano, plain, plane, and plan.

senses.d: A percussive keyboard musical instrument, usually ranging over seven octaves, with white and black colored keys, played by pressing these keys, causing hammers to strike strings.
ex: The piano in his house takes up a lot of space.
She has been taking lessons for many years and now plays piano very well.
Anyhow I pianoed to my own ear, and had no thought at that time for an audience.
John Ashbery, Kenneth Koch, Arnold Weinstein, and others came to the house, taping their poems as I pianoed and zithered and drummed away.

senses.d: To move (the fingers) up and down on, similar to the motions of a pianist playing the piano.
ex: He just stared at her, leaned back in his chair and pianoed his fingers along the tablecloth.
“Jean, it ain't right how you separated those two,” he said, and pianoed the little coffin with his fingers, tapping out his grievance.
Other buildings will also be erected and pianoed by the same architect.
A tabernacle has been built, burnt, rebuilt, electric lighted, organed, pianoed, and frequently filled — all during the last two years.

senses.d: Softly, as a dynamic in a piece of music.

ex: ‘Tradecraft, Chris,’ Enderby put in, who liked his bit of jargon, and Martindale, still piano, shot him a glance of admiration.

senses.d: To become softer and less intense.
ex: “You know, Mrs. Wrigglechops,” pianoed Miss Drucilla , even more meekly and mildly than before, "the ace is either one or eleven."

ety.text: Borrowed from Italian piano. Doublet of plain and plan.
Inherited from Latin plānum, derived from plānus.
Clipping of pianoforte, from Italian pianoforte.
Borrowed from Italian piano, short form of pianoforte. Doublet of plano, chão, and porão.
From French pianiste, from Italian pianista. Analyzable as piano + -ist.

senses.d: A person who plays the piano, particularly with skill or as part of an orchestra.
ex: By the time she became the world's greatest pianist, she had already practised for thousands of hours on her prized piano.
Table IV shows that the pianists were significantly better on both motor and perceptual timing than the nonpianists.

senses.d: A spy using radio or wireless telegraphy to keep in touch with headquarters during the Second World War.

ety.text: Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs)bor. Latin -istalbor. Spanish -ista Spanish pianista From piano (“piano”) + -ista (“-ist”).
From piano (“piano”) + -ista (“-ist”), from Italian piano (“piano; flat”).
